speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the Ministry’s strategy for preventing and mitigating the spread of mpox in Singapore; and (b) what are the applicable precautions and lessons that have been learnt from our whole-of-society effort against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My response will also cover the matters raised in the questions by Ms Joan Pereira1 and Mr Sharael Taha1 which are scheduled for a subsequent Sitting.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have shared our assessment of mpox Clade I and our response plan in a press conference last week.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the less severe mpox Clade II, 15 confirmed cases have been detected this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although there are no Clade I cases in Singapore as yet, we should expect it to arrive here at some point as it spreads beyond Africa.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every pandemic is different – I have to keep emphasising that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to respond according to the characteristics of the virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The key characteristics of mpox Clade I based on what we know so far, are as follows.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is mainly through close physical contact with infected persons, such as sexual contact, mouth-to-mouth, skin-to-skin and skin-to-mouth contact.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Africa, it appears to be family members living in the same household as the primary cases, who are infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We cannot rule out mpox spreading through the air, but based on current evidence, even if it does, it does not spread far and wide like COVID-19 – like one person gives a speech and many members of the audience can get infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is no evidence showing that mpox Clade I or Clade II spreads that way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But this is something we will continue to watch and which should become clearer in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This means that every 10 infected persons will spread the disease to an average of 13 persons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is less infectious than other diseases such as COVID-19 with an R value of five, or chickenpox with an R value of 12.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Out of every 100 cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), there were about three to four fatalities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a concerning number, similar to COVID-19 when it first broke out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it comes here, the case fatality rate will most likely be lower because first, the recorded number in DRC probably has a larger denominator base of undetected cases; so the fatality rate should be lower.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, there will be better access to quality medical care in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Evidence also shows that smallpox vaccination renders cross-protection against mpox.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since smallpox vaccination was required in Singapore up till early 1981, there will be some immunity among a large segment of Singaporeans aged 45 and above.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fourth, specific groups that will be especially affected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One group includes the weak and vulnerable, such as the old, sick or the immunocompromised.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, a large proportion of cases and deaths in DRC are in children below the age of 15.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of this is due to socioeconomic reasons, such as malnutrition or that the children are already afflicted with certain diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We believe that the clinical outcomes will be different in countries outside Africa and we are paying close attention to the risks amongst children.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Based on the current evidence, we are not dealing with a respiratory virus like COVID-19 that required extensive safe management measures, much less a circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That brings me to the key aspects of our response plan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have retained digital declarations for travellers coming into Singapore using the SG Arrival Card.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Several Members have asked me why do we keep that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because such outbreaks will happen from time to time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have, however, adjusted the questions, so that travellers are now required to declare mpox-related symptoms and travel history on the SG Arrival Card.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have put in place temperature and visual screening for travellers arriving from higher risk areas, at both air and sea checkpoints.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As mpox has a long incubation period of up to 21 days, cases may not be picked up at the borders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They may seek medical help later when they turn ill in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we have notified our doctors to be on the alert to spot and immediately report any suspected mpox Clade I cases to the Ministry of Health (MOH).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All suspected mpox Clade I cases will be conveyed to designated hospitals for further assessment and testing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If tested positive, these patients will be isolated in healthcare facilities until they are no longer infectious.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Based on what we currently know of the Clade I virus, our existing hospital capacity, including the intensive care units (ICUs), remains adequate to treat and isolate infected cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Contact tracing will be conducted for all confirmed cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The National Environment Agency will oversee environmental cleaning and disinfection for places visited by the infected persons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Close contacts of Clade I cases will be quarantined in a designated government quarantine facility for up to 21 days from their last date of exposure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have been working closely with the Ministry of Education and Early Childhood Development Agency on contingency plans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Schools have existing protocols to manage outbreaks, such as for hand-foot-and-mouth disease, which are relevant in an mpox Clade I outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include ensuring good hygiene practices and screening students for symptoms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cases will only be allowed to return to school once fully recovered and no longer infectious.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Premises will be cleaned and contact tracing of students and staff will be conducted promptly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If necessary, outbreak management measures, including temporary closure of a class, a level or a school, may be implemented to contain disease spread.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is more effective to focus our vaccination on healthcare workers who need to care for mpox patients, and on close contacts of infected persons as a form of post-exposure vaccination to suppress the transmission of the virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Based on this vaccination approach, our existing supply of vaccines are projected to be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To better strengthen our preparedness and resilience, MOH is also looking at procuring more doses when available.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At present, we do not recommend wearing a mask for people who are well, given that the primary mode of transmission is close physical contact.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, should there be evidence of significant respiratory transmission, such as outside of households, MOH will consider implementing masking on public transport, and in crowded indoor settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our current mask stockpiles and local manufacturing capabilities will assure us of adequate supply.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is unlike COVID-19 that will lead to widespread safe management measures or even a circuit breaker, very unlikely.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Exercising personal responsibility, especially when symptomatic, and practising good personal hygiene, remain effective at reducing the risk of transmission of mpox in the general population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The situation is evolving and there is still some uncertainty around the disease characteristics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will learn more about the disease in the coming months and should be prepared to change our plans as we understand the disease more.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to make the mpox vaccine available and free for vulnerable groups of the population, such as the elderly, who may not have taken the smallpox vaccine previously or immunocompromised patients?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most older Singaporeans would have taken the smallpox vaccine at birth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The coverage before 1981 has been very broad – well over 90%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We think this is better use of the stock of JYNNEOS that we have to suppress transmission, as opposed to offering it widely and free to the population, because given the characteristics of this virus with an R of 1.3, I think our method, our vaccination strategy will be more effective, given the stockpile of JYNNEOS that we have.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wanted to follow up by asking whether the Ministry is planning to implement enhanced surveillance and precautionary measures in close-quarter living environments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means a closer watch-out for symptoms and able to have in situ isolation facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, in all those settings that the Member mentioned, those contingency plans have been developed since COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I wish to ask if information will be put out to the population here so that people can be encouraged to quickly seek medical attention immediately if they exhibit symptoms of mpox, so that it can be quickly picked up by our general practitioners (GPs) and medical professionals.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On that related note, will the Minister consider a community monitoring and surveillance programme or strategy to detect any cases in the population if the situation becomes serious?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the first question, I think in the coming weeks and months, especially when we have our first case, we do expect it to arrive at some point, we will have to put out more information for people to watch out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not difficult to miss because you will start to get lesions on your skin.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think people will be quite concerned.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because of a long incubation period, I think it is not practical to detect and be able to isolate people at the borders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many will be incubating and will go through our checkpoints before they exhibit symptoms and are picked up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, remember the main characteristic of this virus that we are dealing with is a R of 1.3.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while someone is incubating, our memory is always focused on the last crisis and our memory is COVID – someone incubating; no symptoms can spread to 10, 20 people and we have many of those clusters.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this case, it does not look like a virus that exhibits those characteristics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, it is an R of 1.3 which means even if you are incubating, even if you infect someone, it is through very close physical contact.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in Africa, those tends to be their family members, immediate family members that spend a lot of time with you, with physical skin-to-skin touch and physical contact, living together in the same household.
